segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Machinery of Injustice

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, passionate look at one of the great novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to move through Dickens's novel chapter by chapter, passage by passage — trying to understand what makes it so extraordinary.
The fog. The law. The slums. The secrets. The human beings caught in the machinery of all four.
To help us do this properly, I've gathered three guests whose company I find endlessly stimulating — and who could not be more different from one another.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a watch — with total attention to how every mechanism fits together.
She has a gift — rare in academia — for making craft feel thrilling rather than technical.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — he sees the law courts, the philanthropists, the great houses, and asks: who does this serve, and who pays the price?
He earns his anger with evidence, and Bleak House gives him a great deal of evidence to work with.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — comes to every novel as a performer first.
He hears the rhythms, catches the comic timing, and knows when to let silence do the work.

In this opening segment, we're looking at some of the novel's most striking passages: the fog, the slum, the coiled menace of Tulkinghorn, and the first signs of Richard Carstone beginning to unravel.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because the passage that opens our discussion is one of the most viscerally awful things in the novel.
It really is. Tom-all-Alone's. Even the name is doing extraordinary work before we've read a word of the description.
But then Dickens gives us the place itself, and it is genuinely one of the most controlled pieces of gothic horror in nineteenth-century prose.
What strikes me immediately is the narrative choice: we see Tom-all-Alone's through Snagsby — a respectable, timid, London stationer.
He's not a sheltered aristocrat encountering poverty for the first time. He has lived in London all his life.
Dickens uses that detail to devastating effect. Listen to the passage:

"a villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water — though the roads are dry elsewhere — and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses"
That parenthetical — though the roads are dry elsewhere — is the killer move.
It tells us this squalor is not weather, not accident — it is a condition maintained by the city, by the system, specifically for these people.
And then the descent: Snagsby feels as if going deeper, every moment, into an infernal gulf. It's structured as a journey into hell, and Dickens means us to feel that quite literally.
Eleanor is absolutely right to press on that parenthetical, because it is the ideological heart of the passage.
The roads are dry elsewhere. That word elsewhere is doing enormous political work.
Tom-all-Alone's is not a natural disaster. It is a product — manufactured by the indifference of the courts, the landlords, the entire apparatus of Victorian property law.
Dickens understood — perhaps more viscerally than he could articulate theoretically — that Chancery and Tom-all-Alone's are the same system seen from two different ends.
The legal fog at the top produces the physical mud at the bottom. One is the cause; the other is the consequence.
And the novel doesn't let Snagsby — or the reader — simply observe this from a safe distance. He descends into it. He sickens.
What I keep coming back to — as a performer — is that Bucket has the bull's-eye lamp.
He illuminates the horror precisely so that Snagsby — and we — cannot look away. There is something deeply theatrical about that.
Dickens was a man of the theatre. He understood spotlight. He understood what it means to force an audience to see.
And the prose rhythm in that passage — undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water — it's a list that builds like a drumbeat.
You feel the accumulation of it. Each word adds another layer of muck. It is, technically speaking, magnificent.
That sense of accumulation — of things piling up, of descent — runs through so much of this novel.
And it's not only physical. Richard Carstone, Eleanor — you have a passage that shows the same kind of sinking, but from the inside.
Yes, and this passage breaks my heart every time I read it — because Richard knows exactly what is happening to him.
He confesses to Esther — with what Dickens calls his frankest and most feeling manner — and it is the confession of someone who can diagnose his own ruin but cannot stop it.
Here is what he says — and the syntax itself enacts the breakdown:

"I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt, and —"
That trailing dash. He can't finish the sentence. Because to finish it would be to name what he is losing — Ada, his future, himself.
The broken sentence is not careless writing. It is some of the most precise psychology in Victorian fiction.
What I find crucial in that passage is the phrase like grim death. He would have held on — but to what? To a career the system forced on him.
Richard has no inheritance until Jarndyce is settled. He is structurally unable to plan a life, because the law has consumed the resources that would make a life possible.
His inconstancy is not a character flaw in the ordinary sense. It is Chancery externalised — the endless deferral of the court becoming the endless drift of the man.
Dickens shows us a system that makes its victims blame themselves for the damage it does to them. That is the deeper cruelty.
Daniel, that's exactly right — and yet Dickens gives Richard such warmth, such charm, that you grieve for him even as you watch him make every wrong choice.
The confession to Esther works because Richard is not making excuses. He is genuinely bewildered by himself.
Somehow, I mean something that I can't very well express, but you'll make it out — that little aside is heartbreaking.
He trusts Esther to understand him better than he understands himself. And she does. And we do. And the novel breaks your heart with it.
From the fog of the slum and the fog inside Richard's mind — let's move to another kind of fog entirely: the perfectly controlled menace of Tulkinghorn.
Eleanor, you have two passages involving Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock that feel almost like scenes from a stage thriller.
They are theatrical in the most precise sense — Dickens is staging a power struggle using the grammar of physical space.
Lady Dedlock moves toward the door — she refuses to be controlled. And Tulkinghorn stops her without moving a muscle.
Listen to how Dickens frames it:
"Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
Without himself stirring hand or foot or raising his voice. That is the masterstroke. The threat is delivered at absolute stillness.
The violence is entirely in the words — and in what Tulkinghorn knows. Power, here, is information.
And then in the companion passage, he tells her exactly what kind of power he has accumulated:
"I would as soon have hoped to root up by means of my own strength and my own hands the oldest tree on this estate as to shake your hold upon Sir Leicester."
The tree metaphor is extraordinary — it acknowledges the enormity of what he has done, even as he does it.
He is not boasting. He is, in his awful way, being precise — and that precision is more terrifying than any rage could be.
I have read Tulkinghorn aloud more times than I care to count — and that stillness Eleanor describes is the central performance challenge.
Every instinct as an actor tells you to do something when you deliver a threat. Tulkinghorn does nothing. And that nothing must be audible.
Dickens writes him as a man who has so thoroughly internalised power that he no longer needs to perform it.
The alarm-bell line is extraordinary because it's the one moment where the mechanism is made visible — where Tulkinghorn allows us to see the machinery he operates.
And what is that machinery? It is the machinery of reputation, of social standing, of a class system that depends on surfaces remaining intact.
Tulkinghorn's power over Lady Dedlock is not simply that he knows her secret. It's that the secret would destroy her only in this particular social world — a world built on exactly such fictions.
He even hesitates, he tells her — not from mercy, but because the blow might be too severe even for a man who serves Sir Leicester's interests.
That hesitation is the most damning thing. The system spares no-one — not even those who run it.
Fog. Mud. Broken sentences. The quiet menace of a man who never raises his voice. We've covered an enormous amount of ground in just these opening passages.
What strikes me is that all three of you have returned, from different angles, to the same idea: that in Bleak House, the system is the fog — and the fog gets into everything.
We'll continue to trace that fog in the next segment — but for now, Eleanor, Daniel, Oliver: thank you.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Deep Dive: The Anatomy of Richard's Fall

utterances.text: We turn now to one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs: the slow unravelling of Richard Carstone.
Richard is young, charming, genuinely lovable — and yet from almost the first chapter, Dickens plants the seeds of his destruction.
Today we're looking at a cluster of scenes from early in the novel, when hope still feels possible — and when the warnings are already sounding.
Eleanor, you've written about the architecture of character arcs in fiction — where does Richard's story begin, structurally speaking?
It begins, I think, in that scene where Richard and Ada confess their love to Esther — and what's remarkable is how Dickens weights it.
Esther is placed between them — literally, physically — and she becomes the novel's instrument of clear-eyed assessment.
She tells us something that sounds tender but is actually a structural diagnosis — listen to how she frames it:

"It could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Three abstract nouns stacked like load-bearing columns: constancy, fortitude, perseverance.
Dickens is telling us, in the very moment of tenderness, exactly what Richard will fail to supply.
And what I love — what gets me every time — is that Esther immediately adds: 'I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself.'
That little parenthesis is pure Dickens — it humanises the narrator, gives us the warmth, and then the structural irony hits harder because of it.
You're drawn in by the delight, and then the weight of 'constancy, fortitude, perseverance' lands like a verdict.
And Richard says he'll work his fingers to the bone for Ada — which is the most Richard thing imaginable.
Magnificent intention, absolutely no mechanism to execute it.
There's something I want to press on there, because Richard's failure isn't purely personal — it has a structural cause.
He is a ward of Chancery — which means the system has already determined that his energies should wait upon a lawsuit rather than be directed toward any real vocation.
And Jarndyce sees this with absolute clarity — his advice to Richard is almost desperate in its urgency.
He says — and I think this is one of the great speeches in the novel:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
That image of the heathen waggoner — someone who prays for rescue but does nothing to free his own wheel from the mud — is aimed directly at what Richard will become.
He will wait for Jarndyce and Jarndyce to deliver him — and that waiting will hollow him out.
And Jarndyce keeps pushing — the next line is even more specific about what Richard lacks.
He says: "If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts —"
"— leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
The rhetorical structure is extraordinary — that accumulation of 'ever was or could be, ever will or can be' has the rhythm of a legal incantation.
Jarndyce uses the very grammar of certainty to warn against false certainty.
And Richard, we suspect, hears the words without receiving them.
Oliver, you've performed more of Jarndyce's speeches than most people have read them — how does that earlier, tenderer scene with Richard and Ada feel from inside the text?
It's a beautiful, slightly heartbreaking comedy of good intentions — and Jarndyce's voice has this particular texture of tenderness mixed with anxiety.
He tells them he had contemplated their union, but — and this is where performance matters — the repetition of 'afar off' is everything:
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together."
"But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
Three times — 'afar off, afar off, afar off' — and each time the distance in his voice grows.
He wanted this for them, but not yet — and we begin to feel that 'not yet' may mean never.
Jarndyce is extraordinary in this scene precisely because he refuses the easy comfort.
He says, almost against himself: I assume you will remain constant, but if you change, come and tell me — there is nothing shameful in change.
The passage is remarkable — he describes love as a 'chain of flowers' that can too easily become a 'chain of lead.'
"It is well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken, or it might become a chain of lead."
That is not a romantic image — that is a warning about the way sentimental attachment becomes a trap.
And for Richard, tethered to a lawsuit and to an ideal of Ada that he cannot live up to, the chain of lead is exactly what it becomes.
And the confirmation of what Richard actually is — not what he hopes to be — comes from an unexpected quarter: Mrs. Badger.
She is supposedly a figure of mild social comedy, but Dickens gives her the most clinically accurate diagnosis of Richard in the novel.
She tells Esther — with that terrible precision of the well-meaning observer:
"He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a tiresome pursuit."
'A tiresome pursuit.' Delivered with perfect social courtesy — and it is an absolute demolition.
Dickens uses the comic register to say the thing that Esther, or Jarndyce, or Ada could never bring themselves to say directly.
The contrast with Woodcourt is the killer blow, isn't it?
Mrs. Badger says men like Woodcourt take medicine 'from a strong interest in all that it can do.'

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
The irony is that this is not a flattering description of Woodcourt's life — it's hard, underpaid, unglamorous.
But it is the description of a person with a self.
Richard has no such self — only expectations.
And that is not a moral failing in isolation — it is what Chancery produces.
The suit has told Richard since childhood that somewhere in the future there is a fortune waiting for him — why would a person with that belief build a self?
Dickens understands that hope — the wrong kind of hope, passive hope — is not a comfort.
It is a form of slow poisoning.
Which brings us to one of the most beautiful and terrible images in these early chapters — the moment when Richard and Ada walk away from Bleak House.
Esther watches them go, and Dickens gives her a passage of almost unbearable precision.
Oliver — would you read it?

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
"It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
The three sentences move from joy to elegy to omen — and the physical room darkening is both literal and the whole novel in miniature.
Dickens knows exactly where Richard is going. He's already written the ending into the light.
The craft of it is almost cruel — 'so young, so beautiful' reads as celebration, but the repetition of 'so' carries a kind of mourning.
And that phrase 'passed away' — Dickens uses the language of death for what is, at this moment, simply two young people leaving a room.
He is encoding Richard's fate in the grammar of the farewell.
That phrase — 'passed away into the shadow' — will haunt the rest of the novel.
We've seen the seeds of Richard's fall planted with extraordinary care: the passive hope, the lack of vocation, the system that encourages both.
After the break, we turn to another dimension of Bleak House's world — the fog of the law, and those who get lost in it.

segments.title: Close Reading: Jo's Testimony and the Voice of the Voiceless

utterances.text: We turn now to one of the most shattering sequences in all of Bleak House — the inquest scene in Chapter Eleven.
A boy named Jo is called to give evidence.
He is illiterate, parentless, and barely recognised by the law as a person capable of swearing an oath.
Daniel, you've written about how this scene functions as a kind of indictment — not just of the law, but of an entire social order.
What Dickens does here is quietly devastating.
He renders Jo's testimony in free indirect style — not as reported speech but as immediate consciousness stripped of grammar.
And the result is that we hear the shape of an existence, not just a deposition.
Listen to how it opens — just the facts, absolutely bare:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words, then four. Dickens could have written a paragraph of exposition and told us less.
This is the system's product — a child produced by total neglect, testifying to his own erasure.
And the grammar enacts the content — that's the masterstroke.
Jo doesn't know he has two names. He doesn't know "Jo" is short for something longer.
And Dickens renders that not in the coroner's words about him, but in his own absent syntax — declarative, stripped, almost staccato.
But then look at what Jo does know.
He says — and this is extraordinary — "Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
No catechism, no schooling, no church. And yet: a broom is a broom, and lying is wrong.
Dickens is constructing a moral argument in the rhythm of the prose itself — that virtue can exist without the institutions that claim to produce it.
I've read this passage aloud more times than I can count, and it never loses its effect.
The capitalised HE is doing something you can only really feel when you speak it.
"Don't know that Jo is short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM."
That capitalisation is Dickens throwing a tiny act of dignity across the page.
The court has no use for Jo. But Dickens insists the word HE deserves a capital letter — this child exists, he has a self.
And set against Jo's testimony is the wonderful Mrs. Piper — who has quite a lot to say and almost nothing to tell.
Oliver, the comic counterpoint here feels almost cruel in its precision.
Mrs. Piper is one of Dickens's glorious comic gargoyles — you could build an entire career playing her.
Dickens tells us flat out: she has "not much to tell." And then gives her the run of the page.
The testimony arrives "chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation" — which is the joke made visible on the page.
She calls the dead man "the plaintive" — insisting on that malapropism across the whole paragraph.
And the child Johnny — who has "repeatually called after him close at his eels" — apparently has not a nerve in his body.
It's preposterous and funny. And Dickens knows exactly why he's placed this torrent right before Jo's terrible simplicity.
The contrast is forensic, not accidental.
Mrs. Piper's testimony — rambling, parenthetical, drenched in neighbourhood prejudice — is accepted by the court.
Jo's testimony — precise, morally coherent, directly relevant — is thrown out.
The law doesn't reject Jo because he's unreliable. It rejects him because he doesn't fit its category of a competent witness.
That's class operating as epistemology — the poor are literally rendered unknowing, their knowledge inadmissible.
Which makes Dickens's narrative intervention afterward so structurally bold.
He steps outside the fiction — the omniscient narrator addresses Jo directly: "Jo, is it thou?"
That biblical register — "thou," "outer darkness" — is not accidental.
Dickens is invoking the language of scripture specifically to ask: whom does this society leave outside the light?
And the answer is given not in argument but in Jo's own words — the one ray of grace the novel allows him.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That double reported quotation — the narrator quoting Jo quoting his own heart — is extraordinarily layered for a single sentence.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos." I can never read that line without stopping for a moment.
And what makes it unbearable is the context — the dead man himself was nearly as destitute as Jo.
The passage tells us that on a cold winter night the man found Jo shivering in a doorway.
"Neither have I. Not one!" — and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
A man with nothing giving what little he has to another man with nothing.
Dickens earns his sentiment here. He earns every drop of it.
And the novel asks us to notice what that act of kindness reveals about the system's failure.
The man asks Jo whether he ever wished to die — that's not small talk, that's a man recognising his own despair in another.
Two people entirely abandoned by every institution — law, church, charity — finding a scrap of solidarity between themselves.
That's not sentiment. That's Dickens documenting what human beings do when everything else has been stripped away.
And it connects directly to the brickmakers' wives — Jenny and Liz — later in the novel.
Jenny says — and this is devastating in a completely different register:
"It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear... we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!"
"If we knew how to say it" — there it is again. The inarticulate poor, in whom feeling runs deeper than language can reach.
That phrase is doing structural work across the whole novel.
Jo can't quite say what will happen to him after death. Jenny can't quite say what grief and love mean to her.
But Dickens can — and does. That's the novelist's act of translation and advocacy in one.
He gives these characters a voice precisely by showing us how thoroughly the world has denied them one.
That tension between what can be felt and what can be said — and what the novelist does in that gap — feels central to what Bleak House is doing.
Coming up, we'll be looking at the novel's great institutional machinery — Chancery, the law, the fog that opens the book — and asking what Dickens builds with all that darkness.

segments.title: Dickens's Savage Comedy and the Bleak House Grotesque

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, where we're working our way through one of the great novels of the English language — chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
Today we're turning to something that makes Bleak House genuinely unlike any other Victorian novel: its comedy.
Not gentle comedy, not consoling comedy — but something savage, grotesque, and occasionally terrifying in its precision.
With me today are three voices who've been living inside this novel with me.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and critic who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — for what makes it run.
Dr. Daniel Rosen brings a cultural historian's eye — he wants to know who the joke is really on, and who profits from the laughter.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than anyone alive — approaches the novel as pure performance.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because the Bleak House grotesque has a very particular flavour, and I think you hear it before anyone else does.
The thing that strikes you first, when you read this novel aloud, is that the comedy and the horror share the same voice.
Dickens doesn't switch registers between the funny and the dreadful — he uses the same instrument for both.
And nowhere do you feel that more completely than in the old woman in Chancery — the ward who has been waiting, with her documents, for her whole life.
Richard calls her mad, and she turns on him — and listen to this, because Dickens writes it with such extraordinary compression:
"I was a ward myself. I was not mad at that time. I had youth and hope. I believe, beauty. It matters very little now."
And then she continues — and this is where Dickens does something almost impossibly good:
"Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
Those single-word sentences — each one a full stop, each one a year of her life — they're heartbreaking and absurd in the same breath.
What you're describing is Dickens deploying a very specific structural technique — what I'd call compressed enumeration used as elegy.
Each item in the list — youth, hope, beauty — is discarded in a single clause, and then the list continues past where any list should go.
Into Judgment Day. Into the apocalypse. And it sounds perfectly rational — which is precisely the horror.
What Dickens understands is that Chancery doesn't need to be fantastical to seem monstrous — it already is.
The woman's logic is entirely coherent, given what the court has already done to her life.
The comedy collapses back into tragedy not because Dickens signals a shift — but because he never lets you forget they were the same thing all along.
And we should notice who she is, in terms of the system — she was a ward.
She entered Chancery exactly as Ada and Richard are about to enter it — with youth, with hope, with claims she believed would be honoured.
What the novel is showing us is not an eccentric exception — she is the destination.
She's what the institution produces. She is the output of the machine, not a malfunction of it.
The comedy, if that's what we call it, is the comedy of pure institutional logic working perfectly.
That idea of the institution producing its own grotesques is everywhere in the novel — and nowhere more brilliantly managed than with Mr. Vholes.
Vholes is one of the great comic monsters of English fiction, and the genius of it is that he is treated, by everyone in the legal world, as a perfectly respectable man.
And then Dickens shows us how that respectability functions as a weapon — through Mr. Kenge's magnificent defence of the indefensible:

"Repeal it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes?"
And then the killer blow — delivered in Kenge's most fulsome parliamentary manner:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
The argument is: Vholes must be protected because Vholes is respectable, and Vholes is respectable because he must be protected.
It's a perfectly circular system, and Dickens renders it in a perfectly circular sentence. The form enacts the content.
What's so technically beautiful about the Vholes passages is that Dickens is satirising not just the content of the argument but the style of it.
That mock parliamentary transcript — question and answer, question and answer — builds with a kind of horrible inevitability.
Every question is perfectly reasonable. Every answer is perfectly evasive. And then the final answer proves fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
Dickens is showing us how bureaucratic language is itself a form of violence — it sounds like reason but functions as obstruction.
And the comedy is that the obstruction works. Every time. Reliably. For a decade.
What makes Vholes so precise as a satirical figure is the way Dickens shows his language functioning as a performance of duty rather than a discharge of it.

There's that extraordinary passage where Vholes explains, in his most dispassionate inward manner, that he has a professional obligation to be honest — and that the honesty cannot even be billed to anyone.
Listen to how he phrases it — and notice what he's doing:
"I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
He's presenting his candour as a species of virtue — and then immediately pivoting to tell Richard that his affairs are in a very bad way and his marriage was ill-advised.
The brutality is wrapped in a procedural formality so precise it functions as armour.
And then — immediately — "Am I here, sir? Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of some agreeable conversation."
The man has just destroyed Richard's future and pivots to pleasantries in the same breath. It's monstrous. And it's very funny.
That pivot is one of the great comic-horrifying moments in the novel — and it's entirely in the punctuation.
The exclamation mark on "Yes, I thank you" — after everything that's just been said — does all the work.
Now — the Smallweed family operates on a rather different register of comic grotesque.
Where Vholes is cold and procedural, the Smallweeds are — well, they're purely mercenary and they make no attempt whatsoever to disguise it.
When Inspector Bucket whispers to Jarndyce about the will — and how the family handled it — the comedy is almost Jonsonian in its ferocity:

"Hadn't settled how to make their market of it. Quarrelled and hinted about it. First the avaricious grandchildren split upon him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably long, and then they split on one another."
And then Bucket delivers the verdict on the whole family with one of Dickens's most perfectly shaped sentences:
"There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
The exception is the exception only because she's too far gone to be wicked. That's Dickens at full tilt.
What's architecturally interesting about that sentence is that it builds toward what looks like an exception — and then the exception turns out to be no exception at all.
It's a sentence that produces a kind of moral trapdoor.
You think you're about to be reassured — and then the floor drops away.
And Dickens does this again and again — he puts the structure of the joke in service of a moral argument about what these people actually are.
And the Smallweeds are important precisely because they aren't anomalies — they're the logical conclusion of a world in which money and documents are the only real relationships.
The Chancery suit has been running so long that a whole family has organised its emotional life entirely around the will.
What Dickens is giving us in the grotesque characters — the Smallweeds, Vholes, the mad ward in Chancery — is capitalism's work shown clearly.
The comedy is the form in which the truth becomes visible — it's the pressure valve that also reveals the pressure.
And it's worth noting one more Dickensian stroke in all of this — the shadow.
The Mrs. Snagsby passage is different in register — less the ferocious comedy of Vholes or the Smallweeds, more a sustained gothic joke.
Dickens describes her as a ghostly shade, frilled and night-capped, and then he builds this extraordinary sentence:
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
And then the warning — which is also somehow funny and absolutely not funny:
"For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
The marriage vow used as gothic surveillance — it's grotesque domesticity of the highest order.
The anaphora in that passage — "hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own" — is doing something very precise.
The repetition creates a kind of incantation — the sentence won't let you escape, just as Snagsby can't escape her.
And then Dickens turns the biblical formula — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh — which is a covenant of love, into a covenant of dread.
The sacred language is deployed to describe a haunting. That inversion is the engine of the whole passage.
What strikes me across all of these passages is that the comedy never gives you a safe place to stand — it implicates you as a reader even as it makes you laugh.
We're laughing at Vholes's clients — but Dickens keeps pressing: you're also a client of these systems.
Eleanor, Daniel, Oliver — thank you for taking the comedy of this novel as seriously as it deserves.
We'll be back shortly to look at what Dickens does when the comedy falls silent entirely — and what's left in the quiet.

segments.title: Deep Dive: Class, Capital, and the Chancery's Appetite

utterances.text: We turn now to what I think is the novel's most scalding argument — the machinery beneath the surface.
Bleak House is many things — a mystery, a love story, a Gothic inheritance tale.
But underneath all of that, it is a sustained and merciless anatomy of how institutions devour lives.
Daniel Rosen is our guide here — a cultural historian who reads the novel as a map of class power and systemic violence.
Daniel, I want to start with one of Dickens's most extraordinary moments of pure polemic — the narrator stepping forward in chapter thirty-nine to describe the English law.
Yes — and it's worth sitting with how radical this passage is, even by Dickens's standards.
The narrator doesn't hint, doesn't satirise obliquely.
He simply states what the law is for.
Listen to this:
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
And he goes further — "There is no other principle distinctly, certainly, and consistently maintained through all its narrow turnings."
This isn't comedy.
It is a diagnosis — delivered with the deadpan precision of someone who has given up pretending the system is broken.
He's saying: the system works exactly as designed.
What strikes me structurally is that Dickens places that passage in the middle of the novel — not at the start, not at the end.
By chapter thirty-nine, we have already watched Richard Carstone eroded — spiritually, financially, physically — by Chancery.
So when Dickens drops this thesis statement into the narration, it lands not as abstract argument but as confirmation.
We have seen the evidence.
And then that final, devastating sentence — the sardonic comfort he offers.
"Surely they will cease to grumble."
It's the most vicious full stop in the novel.
Eleanor's right — and reading it aloud, you feel the register shift completely.
The narrator has been warm, funny, morally engaged.
And then suddenly he is cold as iron.
Which is the right tone, because what he's describing is not an accident of history — it's a machine.
And that coldness carries into Tulkinghorn, who is the machine's perfect human embodiment.
Tulkinghorn is the figure I keep returning to, because he reveals something the novel understands about power that even Marx might have admired.
He doesn't possess power in the crude sense — he serves the Dedlocks, ostensibly.
But he hoards information, and information is the real currency.
The passage at the deathbed of Nemo is extraordinary in this respect.
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
He has shown nothing but his shell — that is the precise word Dickens uses.
A man who is only his function — who has so thoroughly surrendered his interior life to the system that nothing personal remains.
That is what the law produces in those who serve it most faithfully.
The musical instrument metaphor is doing so much work, isn't it.
A musical instrument is the most interior of objects — it's defined entirely by what it produces, the sound it gives.
And with Tulkinghorn, that interior is inaccessible — permanently.
Dickens is showing us that the law doesn't just distort human relationships — it hollows out the human being who administers it.
And the staging of it matters enormously.
Tulkinghorn stands apart from the surgeon, from the grieving old man, from the little crazy woman at the deathbed.
Three kinds of human response to death — professional, religious, terrified — and he inhabits none of them.
He is simply present, recording, waiting.
It's one of the most quietly terrifying images in Victorian fiction.
And yet beside that coldness, Dickens places one of the most tender passages in the novel — the lament over Nemo's body.
Daniel — you wanted to bring this passage to the table.
Yes — because this is where Dickens does something the pure polemicist never could.
He makes us feel the cost — not in argument, but in imaginative grief.
Nemo has died alone, unknown, without a name that anyone will remember.
And Dickens asks us to imagine him as he once was — a child held at his mother's breast.
"If this forlorn man could have been prophetically seen lying here by the mother at whose breast he nestled, a little child, with eyes upraised to her loving face..."
"what an impossibility the vision would have seemed!"
The poverty and the anonymity that the system produces — Dickens insists we understand it as a theft.
A theft of the life this man should have lived.
And then he turns the knife with one extraordinary question.
"Oh, if in brighter days the now-extinguished fire within him ever burned for one woman who held him in her heart, where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!"
An exclamation point masquerading as a question.
He knows the answer.
We don't yet — but we will.
That's the architecture of the whole novel working in a single sentence.
Dickens plants the question before we can possibly understand its full weight.
And when the answer arrives — when we learn who Lady Dedlock is to Nemo — every tender detail here becomes retrospectively unbearable.
The word 'ashes' is doing enormous work — because she is already burning too.
That theme of sacrifice consumed from within — it reaches back deep into the Dedlock family history.
Daniel, you were drawn to the Gothic passage Mrs. Rouncewell narrates in chapter seven — the story of the first Lady Dedlock.
It's a story about what happens when a woman's allegiance to her own family is punished by the family she married into.
Her brother has been killed by Sir Morbury's kinsman in the Civil War.
And her response is sabotage — she lames the Royalist horses in the night.
But of course the violence turns back on her.
"She was lamed in the hip and from that hour began to pine away."
And that phrasing — 'from that hour' — is exact.
Her resistance to the system — the dynastic marriage, the aristocratic cause — is punished by permanent physical diminishment.
Dickens writes the class structure into the body itself.
There's something irresistible about the way Rouncewell tells it, though.
She 'gravely nods and continues' — that grave nod is marvellous.
She is the repository of the family's dark history, dispensing it with the solemnity of a keeper of relics.
And yet the story she tells is almost operatic — the husband catching her in the stall, the frightened horse, the fall.
Dickens is letting Gothic fiction colonise the family history — and showing us that the aristocracy has always needed that darkness to sustain its glamour.
And it rhymes so precisely with the later story of Lady Dedlock's sister — Esther's mother's sister, Miss Barbary.
The passage Jarndyce recounts to Esther in chapter forty-three is extraordinary — she too chooses a form of self-laming.
She writes to Boythorn, the man who loves her, and in the letter she simply annihilates herself.
"She wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did."
"She made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it."
'Live in it and die in it' — that is a sentence of extraordinary compression.
The sacrifice is not an act but a dwelling place — she inhabits it for the rest of her life.
And the engine of that sacrifice is the aristocratic honour code — which Dickens is careful to name.
She makes the sacrifice because of his 'proud temper and his strained sense of honour' — but Jarndyce adds one devastating qualifier.
'Which were both her nature too.'
She doesn't merely submit to a code imposed from outside.
She has internalised it so completely that she enforces it against herself.
That is the most complete form of domination — when the oppressed become their own instrument of oppression.
And yet against all of that — the law, the honour code, the Gothic inheritance — Dickens places Ada beside Richard.
The image in chapter fifty-one is almost unbearably simple.
"My darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me."
Against everything the system has produced — the sacrifice, the secrets, the pining away — that gesture.
It doesn't answer Dickens's argument.
But it insists there is something the system cannot take.
That tension — between the machine and the human gesture that survives it — may be the deepest thing this novel does.
Thank you, Daniel, Eleanor, Oliver — we'll carry all of this into our next section.

segments.title: The Secret Unravels: Lady Dedlock's Arc and Narrative Revelation

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart, passage by passage, to see how it works.
I'm joined today by three brilliant readers: Eleanor Hartley, who teaches creative writing and thinks in sentences the way architects think in load-bearing walls.
Daniel Rosen, cultural historian, who reads every institution in a novel as a mechanism of class power — and earns every word of that argument.
And Oliver Trevelyan, actor and audiobook narrator, who hears what the rest of us only read.
Today's segment sits at the novel's nerve centre: the unravelling of Lady Dedlock's secret, and the machinery Dickens uses to keep it in tension.
We have four passages in front of us — and they span the full social range of this novel, from a brickmaker's floor to a Lincolnshire terrace.
Eleanor, I want to start with you — because one of these passages is doing something structurally peculiar, and I suspect you've already spotted it.
Yes — and what strikes me first is how Dickens engineers revelation through indirection.
The letter that Sir Leicester reads aloud in chapter twelve is a perfect example — the secret is conveyed not dramatically but bureaucratically.
Sir Leicester can barely find the right passage in the letter — he fumbles with his eyeglass, loses his place.
And yet the words he finally lands on are devastating to Lady Dedlock, even if he has no idea why.
Listen to how Tulkinghorn phrases it — I want to read this exactly as it appears on the page.
'I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.'
'I have seen him.' Three words — a full stop — and the entire architecture of Lady Dedlock's past comes trembling into view.
Dickens doesn't need an exclamation mark. He barely needs a sentence. The compression is extraordinary.
That compression is what kills you when you read it aloud — because you have to perform Sir Leicester's complete obliviousness at the same moment.
He's proud of himself for finally finding the right postscript, bless him. He has not the faintest notion he is detonating a bomb in his wife's lap.
And then you get the passage describing Tulkinghorn's arrival at Chesney Wold — which is the other side of the same coin.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary description of a man who is all surface and no disclosure. The prose itself mimics that quality.
The passage sets him up like this — and you have to savour every clause.
'He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.'
Every limb, every crease — the man is nothing but secrets, all the way down to the fabric of his coat.
And then Dickens asks the question we most want answered — and refuses to answer it.

'Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.'
He is his own client. That phrase is a complete portrait of a certain kind of professional soul — brilliant, and utterly chilling.
What Oliver's reading makes vivid is that Tulkinghorn isn't just a mysterious individual — he's a structural function.
He is the legal system made flesh: opaque, self-interested, indispensable to the aristocracy precisely because he has no loyalty except to the management of information.
And look at what that information is being used to protect — the reputation of a class that has everything to hide and every instrument of power to hide it with.
The passage where Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock watch each other is the novel's most precise anatomy of that power relation.
The narrator asks what each would give to know how much the other knows — and the answer is: everything.

'Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.'
'Hidden, for the time.' That qualifier is doing enormous work — Dickens knows we know it cannot be hidden forever.

Meanwhile Sir Leicester stares at the fire, thinking nothing of consequence has happened. And that is the class system in miniature — the powerful man entirely insulated from the real drama occurring beside him.
Daniel's point about Sir Leicester and the fire is worth sitting with, because Dickens stages this scene with extraordinary geometric precision.
Three people in a room. Two of them locked in a silent war of mutual surveillance. One of them watching flames and thinking about rights of way.
It's a technique straight out of high drama — the oblivious figure who anchors a scene while the real stakes unfold around him.
And what connects to the identity question — the matter of who Lady Dedlock was before she became Lady Dedlock — is the passage about her in chapter seventeen.
Jarndyce tells Esther what he knows: that the mysterious correspondent claimed to be her aunt, and that she would never disclose more than that.
The phrasing is almost lawyerly in its precision — which makes sense, since every disclosure in this novel is filtered through legal mediation.
'That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose.'
The parenthetical — 'he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution' — is both a characterisation and a warning. This woman will not crack easily.
And then you turn back to the brickmaker passage — and the contrast is almost violent.
Because here is a man who cannot hide anything — who has no secrets, only wounds, and who recites them with furious precision because nobody is listening anyway.
He pre-empts Mrs. Pardiggle's questions — takes them out of her mouth before she can ask them — and the effect is shattering.
This is one of the great passages in the novel for the voice. You have to do it raw.
'Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!'
And then — with barely a breath — he goes further.
'We've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides.'
'So much the better for them.' That is what hopelessness sounds like when it has run out of room for sentiment.
Dickens gives that man a voice that is almost unbearable to perform — because the anger is completely earned and completely without remedy.
Oliver puts his finger on something essential — the brickmaker is Dickens's most uncompromising portrait of what the system actually produces.
Not a pitiable wretch to be reformed by a tract. A man who has looked at the logic of his own life and drawn the only rational conclusions available to him.
He says: I've been drunk for three days. And if I'd had the money, I'd have been drunk four. That is not moral failure — that is a completely coherent response to an incoherent world.
The church? He says he shouldn't be expected there. And he's right — 'the beadle's too gen-teel for me.'
Dickens is making the brickmaker's argument as well as Dickens could ever have made it himself — perhaps better, because he gives it that voice rather than a narrator's sympathy.
Now set that beside Lady Dedlock — whose secret is guarded by lawyers, by silence, by the entire apparatus of class respectability.
The brickmaker has nothing to hide and nowhere to hide it. Lady Dedlock has everything to hide and every institution in England protecting her ability to do so.
What I keep returning to is the formal symmetry between those two worlds — and whether Dickens intends us to feel the connection.
The dual narrative — Esther's first-person account and the omniscient narrator's cold, sweeping view — is precisely designed to hold both worlds in the same frame.
Esther witnesses the brickmaker. The omniscient narrator dissects Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock. We're being asked to hold both in mind simultaneously.
That's the architecture of the whole novel: the fog connects everything, even when the characters themselves cannot see the connections.
The fog as connective tissue — both literal and structural. That is a thought worth sitting with.
We've moved in this segment from a brickmaker's floor to a Lincolnshire terrace to a lawyer's letter — and found the same novel pulling the threads tight.
Eleanor, Daniel, Oliver — thank you. In our next segment, we turn to what the novel does with time, and the peculiar eternity of Chancery.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption and Ruin in the House of Bleak

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end of our journey through the opening world of Bleak House.
And I want to close by asking each of you about what lingers — what the novel leaves us holding.
Because Bleak House doesn't offer easy redemption.
It offers ruin, and tenderness, and a few extraordinary glimpses of human grace amid the wreckage.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with the cold war at Chesney Wold.
What strikes me about those scenes between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn is the sheer architectural precision of the threat.
Dickens constructs a social surface so perfectly maintained that the violence underneath is almost invisible.
Listen to how he renders that stalemate — this passage is extraordinary.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
"Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
That phrase — "speechless repository of noble confidences" — is almost a legal instrument in itself.
He holds their secrets the way a vault holds money — not for their benefit, but for his own leverage.
And then Dickens reveals what neither of them will say aloud — "what each would give to know how much the other knows" — and seals it with "all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
Eleanor is right that it's architectural — but I'd say the architecture is a cage, and Lady Dedlock built it herself.
She chose the title, the marriage, the performance of the "exhausted deity."
But Tulkinghorn is the system made flesh — he accumulates secrets as capital, and he will spend them when the return is greatest.
What interests me is what that secrecy costs — in human terms — at the bottom of the same system.
Think of Nemo, dying in that room — and this is one of the most damning portraits of poverty Dickens ever wrote.
"Through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium."
Notice that the opium enters Tulkinghorn's mouth — not Nemo's.
The law tastes what poverty produces — and still does nothing.
That detail is devastating — and Daniel, you've put your finger on exactly why that scene works so well as theatre.
Dickens puts the sensation inside the observer — not the sufferer.
It's a profoundly theatrical trick: we experience Nemo's degradation through the clean man's body.
But the moment that gets me — every time I read it aloud — is Jo.
After all that gothic darkness around Nemo's death, Dickens gives us this small boy wiping his eyes with his wretched sleeve.
"He wos wery good to me," says the boy.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The spelling itself is the argument — it places Jo outside standard language, outside the system that writes its laws in a script he cannot read.
And yet the sentiment is the purest in the novel.
Oliver, that's exactly right — and it rhymes with something I find unbearable in Richard Carstone.
Because Richard is articulate — fully literate, educated, inside the system — and Chancery destroys him just as completely.
He even diagnoses his own ruin.
"If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn't settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything."
"And yet that's my unhappy case. I was born into this unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it has gone on unsettling me ever since."
"Born into" — that's the killer phrase.
It's not a failure of character — it's an inheritance, a condition, a sentence passed before he drew breath.
That's the structural argument of the entire novel, compressed into one young man's confession.
Jo cannot read; Richard can articulate his predicament with perfect clarity.
Chancery consumes both of them with equal indifference.
That's what makes Bleak House so unsparing — it's not the wicked who suffer.
It's the merely unlucky, the merely born.
And Dickens makes sure we feel that — not just understand it — through the sheer variety of registers he commands.
Gothic, comic, sentimental, legalistic, lyrical — he plays every instrument in the orchestra.
And when he brings it down to a boy with a wretched sleeve, whispering that a dead man was wery good to him — that's when the whole edifice lands.
Eleanor, Daniel, Oliver — this has been a conversation I'll carry with me for a long time.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is that Bleak House refuses its readers easy exits.
The fog doesn't lift.
Chancery does not reform.
Jo has no surname, no fixed address, and precious little hope — and Dickens insists we know it.
What the novel does offer — and this feels important — is witness.
It sees everyone.
That is perhaps the most radical thing a novel of this scale can do.
Thank you for joining us on Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back with more episodes — more fog, more Chancery, more of Dickens's astonishing, infuriating, magnificent world.

c22:p51.text:
When they come at last to Tom-all-Alone’s, Mr. Bucket stops for a
moment at the corner and takes a lighted bull’s-eye from the
constable on duty there, who then accompanies him with his own
particular bull’s-eye at his waist. Between his two conductors, Mr.
Snagsby passes along the middle of a villainous street, undrained,
unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water—though the roads
are dry elsewhere—and reeking with such smells and sights that he,
who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses.
Branching from this street and its heaps of ruins are other streets
and courts so infamous that Mr. Snagsby sickens in body and mind and
feels as if he were going every moment deeper down into the infernal
gulf.

c23:p37.text:
We walked a little way without speaking, and presently Richard
addressed me in his frankest and most feeling manner, thus: “My dear
Esther, I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant
sort of fellow. I don’t mean constant to Ada, for I love her
dearly—better and better every day—but constant to myself.
(Somehow, I mean something that I can’t very well express, but you’ll
make it out.) If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have
held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and
should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and
shouldn’t be in debt,  and—”
c23:p37.summary: Richard makes an earnest and heartfelt confession to Esther that he wishes he were more constant, both to himself and to his various professional pursuits, and admits his financial troubles.

c41:p43.text:
Without deigning to rejoin, she moves to the inner door and has it in
her hand when he says to her, without himself stirring hand or foot
or raising his voice, “Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and
hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the
alarm-bell and rouse the house. And then I must speak out before
every guest and servant, every man and woman, in it.”
c41:p43.summary: Tulkinghorn stops Lady Dedlock's exit with a calm threat to ring the alarm-bell and expose her secret to the entire household if she does not comply.

“I declare to you, Lady Dedlock, that with anything short of this
case that I have, I would as soon have hoped to root up by means of
my own strength and my own hands the oldest tree on this estate as to
shake your hold upon Sir Leicester and Sir Leicester’s trust and
confidence in you. And even now, with this case, I hesitate. Not that
he could doubt (that, even with him, is impossible), but that nothing
can prepare him for the blow.”

c13:p99.text:
There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.
c13:p99.summary: Richard and Ada confide to Esther their mutual love, placing themselves on either side of her. Esther counsels them about the demands of enduring love and promises to speak to Mr. Jarndyce.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.
c13:p118.best_quote: Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it.

c13:p113.text:
“Rick,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I am glad to have won your confidence. I
hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us
four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new
interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the
possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don’t be shy, Ada,
don’t be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together.
I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was
afar off, Rick, afar off!”
c13:p113.summary: Mr. Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada, confirming he is glad to have their confidence and that he did contemplate their union as a possibility.
c13:p113.best_quote: When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together. I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.

All I say before speaking to you according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me, Rick!)—don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it.

c12:p116.summary: The passage describes the subsequent meetings of Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn at Chesney Wold; they maintain their social masks while watchfully observing each other, each suspicious of the other's hidden knowledge and prepared for revelation.
c12:p116.best_quote: They meet again at dinner—again, next day—again, for many days in succession. Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine. Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

c10:p66.text:
For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,
lean-ribbed ticking, and coarse sacking, the lawyer, hesitating just
within the doorway, sees a man. He lies there, dressed in shirt and
trousers, with bare feet. He has a yellow look in the spectral
darkness of a candle that has guttered down until the whole length of
its wick (still burning) has doubled over and left a tower of
winding-sheet above it. His hair is ragged, mingling with his
whiskers and his beard—the latter, ragged too, and grown, like the
scum and mist around him, in neglect. Foul and filthy as the room is,
foul and filthy as the air is, it is not easy to perceive what fumes
those are which most oppress the senses in it; but through the
general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco,
there comes into the lawyer’s mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.

“He was wery good to me,” says the boy, wiping his eyes with his
wretched sleeve. “Wen I see him a-layin’ so stritched out just now, I
wished he could have heerd me tell him so. He wos wery good to me, he
wos!”

c23:p41.text:
“You are kinder to me than I often am to myself,” he returned. “My
dear Esther, I am a very unfortunate dog not to be more settled, but
how CAN I be more settled? If you lived in an unfinished house, you
couldn’t settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything
you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to
anything; and yet that’s my unhappy case. I was born into this
unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it began
to unsettle me before I quite knew the difference between a suit at
law and a suit of clothes; and it has gone on unsettling me ever
since; and here I am now, conscious sometimes that I am but a
worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada.”
